candidates.title: A Pop-Up Book Vase Offers Six Looks Without Extra Vases
candidates.full_text:
I am not much of a flower person and, consequently, not much of a flower vase person. As much as I know that they can add to the aesthetic beauty of any space, I don’t have much space to display them or add to my messycore clutter. Also, most flower vase designs don’t appeal to me enough that I’d actually make space for them. But as a certified book lover, anything that’s close to the look of a book is something I might actually consider.

The Pop-up Book Vase is one such flower display that has a certain look I might go for if I decide to buy a few flowers and display them. It uses a book aesthetic where you can turn the page and get a new look with its three-dimensional paper vase silhouette. This way, you get a different look by switching among the three designs if you’re the kind of person who wants something new to look at every once in a while.

The way this vase is designed goes beyond printing a book pattern on a regular vase. The flowers go into a glass test tube, which fits into the book’s spine. Each book has three vase shapes that you can change as you turn the page. Turning the book upside down changes which end of the silhouette is wider, so you get something new again. You basically get six possible configurations of a vase in just one object, rather than six separate containers.

That division between the materials is what makes the idea work. The paper creates the decorative shape, while the glass holds the water. MECLI calls the design Flowery Tale and specifies water-resistant paper, but that doesn’t mean you should treat the whole thing like a waterproof vessel. The brand advises wiping up water promptly and letting the paper dry thoroughly before storing it. I’d still keep the messy part of refilling away from my actual books.

The storage aspect is probably what appeals to me most. MECLI says you can return it to a bookshelf when it’s not in use. The closed book measures approximately 3.9 inches wide, 1.2 inches deep, and 7.2 inches tall. For someone who doesn’t regularly buy flowers, that’s more useful than having an empty vase taking up display space between bouquets. It still needs room when open, of course, so I wouldn’t expect it to magically solve my clutter problem. But I like that it has somewhere to go when the flowers are gone.

It’s also a nice option for someone who wants a small floral gesture rather than a full centerpiece. The test-tube format suggests starting with a single bloom instead of trying to squeeze in a large bouquet. For me, that makes the idea of displaying flowers feel a little less like another decorating project. The page-turning is part of the appeal, too: I’d be choosing a shape to go with the flower rather than buying another vase.

At $45, though, the Pop-up Book Vase is a decorative purchase rather than the cheapest way to display a flower. IKEA’s VILJESTARK, a 6¾-inch glass vase listed at $1.99 in the US, handles the basic job for much less. Its shape stays the same, whereas the Pop-up Book Vase offers changing silhouettes and book-shaped storage. If all you need is a small container for a stem, IKEA makes more financial sense. Here, the extra money is buying the paper construction and the pleasure of changing the display.

I don’t think this would suddenly turn me into someone who always has fresh flowers at home. But it gives me a reason to consider making room for one. A vase that can spend its downtime on a bookshelf feels more suited to my habits than one that needs a permanent spot on the table.

candidates.title: HTD Aquatic GMT: a true GMT diver from Florence
candidates.full_text:
The GMT-Master II look is the most copied silhouette in watches: a two-tone 24-hour bezel, a fourth hand, a watch that keeps two time zones straight while you cross them. Getting the Rolex version takes five figures and a relationship with a dealer. HTD, a small operation working out of a Florence laboratory, will sell you the same working idea for $1,111, shipped from Italy with the duties already covered.

HTD stands for Horological Tools Department. Federico Del Guerra and Federico Zulian founded the brand in Florence in 2020, and the Aquatìc GMT is its first GMT, built on the Aquatìc diver the brand already sells. It’s a small watch with a serious movement inside, and the movement is my favorite part of this one.

The case is 316L stainless steel, 39mm across and 47mm lug to lug, which puts it in the wear-it-every-day class rather than the dinner-plate class. Thickness is 12.4mm including the crystal, a domed sapphire with an internal anti-reflective coating that gives the dial its soft vintage edge. Under it, the watch is still a diver: 200 meters of water resistance and a screw-down crown sealed with four O-rings.

Every version runs the same black dial. Applied hour markers are beveled toward the center, a small three-dimensional touch you notice in daylight, and the lume is Super-LumiNova BGW9 laid down in multiple layers. It glows blue, generously, on the markers and the domed hands. Its date numerals alternate red and black, odd dates in red, a tribute to the way Florence numbers its streets.

Most affordable GMT watches use a caller movement: the 24-hour hand moves and the main hands stay put, which is fine for tracking a second office and wrong for landing in one. The Miyota 9075 inside the Aquatìc is a traveler GMT. Land, pull the crown, and the local hour hand jumps forward or back in clean one-hour steps while the GMT hand keeps home time running untouched.

That’s the trick the GMT-Master made famous, done properly, at a tenth of the price.

Inside, the 9075 runs at 28,800 beats per hour with a 42-hour power reserve, and HTD regulates every single unit in its Florence workshop before it ships. A microbrand at this price usually buys movements by the tray and cases them up. Regulating each one in-house is bench time, and bench time is the thing this segment usually skips.

Its bezel turns in 24 precise clicks on a new ball-bearing mechanism HTD built for this watch, so it lands on each hour with a mechanical certainty you feel through your fingertips. Four versions share the same case, dial, and movement, and the pick is purely about color.

Rosso Blu is the blue-and-red Pepsi, the one that wears its inspiration openly. Golden Brown runs brown with gold tones, the Root Beer configuration, and pairs it with a gold-framed date window. Departure Green goes green. The World Timer swaps the 24-hour scale for a black bezel engraved with city names, Florence among them, so a twist of the bezel lines up a third reference against the GMT hand.

The watch rides on HTD’s 323 bracelet, a three-link steel design the brand refined for its sport watches. Ordering asks for your wrist measurement, the bracelet arrives sized, and any extra links come inside the box. It’s a small touch that saves the usual first-day hunt for a screwdriver.

Look at the World Timer twice if you track more than two zones. Its bezel carries the city ring a travel watch used before phones did the job: line a city up against the GMT hand and that city’s hour reads straight off the bezel, Florence included as the home marker. It’s the quietest of the four and the most old-school in how it works.

Buying is direct. HTD sells the watch from its own store at $1,111, the price holding the same across all four bezels, and US orders carry all tariffs and duties included in that figure. Watches ship by DHL against a signature, and the warranty runs two years and transfers to a second owner if you sell the watch on.

HTD also takes returns inside 14 days on a prepaid DHL label for buyers who change their minds. The GMT is in stock now, with deliveries running since late October, and the brand’s laboratory in Florence handles sizing, engraving requests, and service under one roof. Delivery runs three to seven business days once the watch ships.

What you give up is the name on the dial and everything that trails behind it: the dealer theater, the resale premium, the recognition at a glance.

What you keep is the function that made the GMT-Master famous

candidates.title: Micro Journal Rev.2.1.MINI Writing Laptop Pairs a Wide Screen With Just 48 Keys
candidates.full_text:
Opening a laptop to write a paragraph can quickly turn into checking messages, rearranging windows, and forgetting the sentence you had in mind. The Micro Journal Rev.2.1.MINI, nicknamed Baby Shark, puts writing at the center of a small, folding computer instead. Its wide screen and compact mechanical keyboard give your words their own space, while Linux supplies the editing tools beneath that colorful clamshell.

The chunky enclosure doesn’t try to resemble a slim aluminum laptop. A bright red shell, dark panels, exposed screws, and ridged side knobs give it the character of a little workshop instrument. Its hinged display folds down over the keyboard when you’re finished. The 3D-printed construction makes color part of the customization, rather than limiting everyone to another black rectangle in their bag.

The 8-inch LCD is unusually wide and shallow, with a 1280×400 resolution that stretches a document across the device. It leaves space for your passage without offering the vertical expanse of a conventional laptop screen. That’s a useful distinction for drafting: there’s room to work through a sentence, but reviewing several pages still means scrolling rather than shrinking everything into an overview.

The keyboard makes a similar trade. Its 48 keys form a four-row, 12-column grid, rather than the staggered rows most typists know. Numbers and additional symbols live on layers accessed by holding another key, which keeps the footprint small while asking your fingers to learn new combinations. Vial software lets you remap assignments, and hot-swappable switches let you change the feel without soldering.

A Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W runs Linux inside, with WordGrinder and nano available for drafting and editing. That gives you somewhere to revise yesterday’s work as well as start today’s entry. Files can leave through a USB flash drive or a browser-based interface on your local network, so a writing session doesn’t have to end with retyping everything on your main computer.

Portability also depends on what you put inside. Baby Shark takes up to four replaceable 18650 cells, sold separately, or runs directly from USB power. The connector is USB-C, but the documented setup requires a USB-A charger and a USB-A-to-USB-C cable, not USB Power Delivery. That means the charger already serving your laptop may not be the one this little writing machine needs.

Linux brings a pause before the writing starts: the seller estimates about 30 seconds to boot. This isn’t an instant-on notebook, and closing the screen isn’t a substitute for shutting the system down properly. On the other hand, published enclosure files, circuit-board designs, and firmware give owners ways to repair or modify it, instead of treating the device as a sealed appliance.

Baby Shark is sold as a DIY project even when ordered assembled, with no seller warranty. Later batches are planned without the Raspberry Pi, leaving buyers to supply it themselves. There’s considerable room to make both the hardware and software your own, provided that adjusting the keyboard doesn’t become another way to postpone the paragraph you originally sat down to write. There’s also a Purple Black Mint Green, nicknamed Witch, version inspired by the EVA-01 from the famed anime, Evangelion.
